title: HBM and host transfer overhead comparison — A100 / H100 / L40S
content:
Purpose and scope
---
Quick internal benchmark focusing on the host <-> HBM transfer path and small-chunk transfer overheads that materially affect long-context and KV-cache refill latency for streaming generation. Most existing SKU comparisons show aggregate throughput numbers — this note drills into microtransfer latency (4KB/64KB/4MB), driver/CUDA behavior, and how those microcosts amplify in our runtime when doing repeated small KV cache writes or token-by-token restoration.

Motivation / Why this matters
---
- Our runtime’s KV cache refill pattern (many small memcpy-like ops per token for some models/quantized kernels) can become dominated by host<->device transfer overheads instead of raw compute.
- Cloud SKUs vary not only by peak HBM bandwidth but by PCIe/NVLink topology, driver prefetch/stream behavior and NVLink peer-path selection. This causes non-obvious tail-latency differences when running real token-steady inference.

Experimental design
---
Tested SKUs (representative):
- AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100 40GB) — driver 525.85, CUDA 11.8
- GCP a2-megagpu (H100) — driver 535.54, CUDA 12.3
- Azure ND96asrs_v4 (L40s) — driver 545.30, CUDA 12.4

Microbench harness: a small C++/CUDA program (linked in PR) that measures:
- one-shot cudaMemcpy (host->device, device->host) latency for sizes 4KB, 64KB, 4MB; repeated 100k times to get p50/p90/p99.
- cudaMemcpyPeer and cudaMemcpyAsync with explicit pinned host buffers and with pageable host buffers to show UVM overhead.
- NVLink path selection probe: force peer copy and check which GPU path is used (when applicable) using nvidia-smi topo and our trace.
- Simulated KV-cache refill loop: repeated small copies (4KB * 128) per token across CUDA streams to mimic runtime pattern.

End-to-end bench: running a trimmed transformer (1.3B-ish) in our runtime pinned to single-GPU with kv-cache enabled, evaluation traffic with token-steady generation at 8B context and measuring token P50/P90/P99 latencies. We compare two runtime modes: (A) naive per-token cache writes (small-copy heavy), (B) batched cache writes (coalesce into larger transfers).

Driver/CUDA matrix:
- Each SKU tested with at least one contemporary driver/CUDA pair. Where possible we re-ran with an alternate driver (e.g., GCP H100 with 535.54 vs 540.x) to see driver regressions.

Key microbench results (representative numbers, median of 10 runs)
---
Microcopy host->device p50 / p99 (ms)
- 4KB: A100 (0.018 / 0.045), H100 (0.012 / 0.028), L40s (0.025 / 0.069)
- 64KB: A100 (0.12 / 0.21), H100 (0.09 / 0.16), L40s (0.18 / 0.35)
- 4MB: A100 (1.8 / 2.6), H100 (1.2 / 2.1), L40s (2.4 / 3.8)

Notes: p99 numbers have high variance across VMs; we ensured low background noise by draining other workloads and repeating runs. H100 consistently shows lower small-copy latency — likely NVLink improvements and driver-level async DMA optimizations. L40s (Azure) shows higher tail which aligns with observed customer-facing p99 spikes in prior weeks.

UVM/pageable vs pinned host buffers
---
- Using pinned host buffers reduces 4KB p50 by ~40–60% across all SKUs (largest impact on L40s). Pageable (UVM) copies still acceptable for large transfers but are catastrophic at small sizes (p99 increases by 3–4x).

KV-cache simulated refill (per-token pattern)
---
Pattern: 128 independent 4KB writes per token (512KB total), repeated 1024 tokens.
- Naive (no coalescing): observed token p50 inflation of ~60–80% vs the batched baseline; p99 increased by 2–3x on L40s.
- Batched (grouped into 8 x 64KB transfers): token p50 improves ~30–45% and p99 comes down to near single-copy numbers.

End-to-end inference observations
---
- With naive KV writes, observed generator token p50: A100 (6.4ms), H100 (5.2ms), L40s (8.8ms). Token p99: A100 (18ms), H100 (11.6ms), L40s (28ms).
- Switching to coalesced transfers reduced token p50 by ~35% on all SKUs and brought L40s p99 down by ~40% (still higher than H100 baseline).
- Driver upgrades (on H100 from 535.x -> 540.x) showed a modest improvement for large transfers but did not materially change small-copy p99 — suggests small-copy behavior is more pinned to DMA/path and OS interaction than kernel-level bandwidth tuning.

Root cause hypotheses
---
1) Small transfer overhead includes syscall/driver arbitration, pinned-buffer registration, and NVLink/PCIe arbitration; variance across SKUs arises from different PCIe root complex topology and NIC/host CPU interaction.
2) L40s NIC/BIOS defaults on our test images frequently fall back to slightly suboptimal PCIe clocking and bus interleaving for small DMA bursts leading to longer tail latencies.
3) UVM/pageable copies introduce page-fault/resident checks on demand; for repeated small interactions this is significant unless pinned buffers are used.

Practical recommendations for the runtime (short term)
---
- Always use pinned host buffers for KV-cache hot-paths. Add a config toggle default-on for dedicated/dedicated-like deployments.
- Implement small-copy coalescing in the KV write path: group small writes into 64KB-256KB windows before issuing cudaMemcpyAsync. This reduces syscall & DMA overhead and cuts p99 substantially.
- Offer an autoswitch: if observed small-copy rate > X ops/sec, switch to batched writes transparently.
- Expose a runtime diagnostic: live counters for small-copy count, coalesce rate, and measured host->device p99 for small sizes.

Longer-term / infra ops items
---
- Work with infra to validate BIOS/firmware PCIe settings for L40s images (power/clocking, SR-IOV toggles). Document a validated AMI/VM image per cloud SKU with tuned BIOS and driver levels.
- Test alternative driver/CUDA combos for L40s (we suspect later 545.x/550.x may have fixes but observed instability in some runs).
- Consider integrating a GPUDirect RDMA check for multi-GPU cases where host<->device transfer happens via NIC (relevant for multi-host KV syncs).

Open questions / next experiments
---
- Can NVLink peer transfer patterns be exploited further for token steady workloads by pinning specific GPUs to a region of kv-cache to avoid host roundtrips? (Follow-up: small prototype scheduled, owner: Liam)
- Are there hypervisor-level knobs on Azure that explain the L40s tail? Need infra to repro with bare-metal-like instance or run on a different Azure region.
- Run the same small-copy matrix under different Linux kernels to isolate OS vs driver behavior.

Appendix: test artifacts
---
- Benchmark harness and scripts: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/432 (bench/hbm-transfer).
- Raw CSVs (per-run) are uploaded to the shared bucket; request via internal infra job id JIRA-6543.
- Quick how-to to reproduce locally included in PR README (requires root / elevated access for pinned-buffer registration tests).

Concluding note
---
Small host<->HBM transfer costs materially change our real-server p99 for long-context streaming workloads. The most cost-effective mitigations are on the runtime (pinned buffers + coalescing + autoswitch) while infra and driver teams pursue SKU-specific tuning. This doc is a snapshot of the experimental run — next steps are focused prototypes and a small runtime change that toggles coalescing automatically when a high small-copy rate is detected.

Unresolved: need infra to reproduce L40s tail in another region and test alternative drivers; schedule follow-up in next week’s serving-runtime sync.
